title: Security goals and network layers
heading: Follow the request and mark each trust boundary
problem: a browser request traveling from a local network through intermediaries to an application.

attacker position, trust anchor and security goal.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A browser sends an application request inside several envelopes. HTTP supplies the request meaning; TCP supplies a reliable byte stream; IP supplies addresses for routing; and the local link carries a frame to the next device. Each receiving layer processes its own header. Routers usually replace link headers at each hop while forwarding the IP packet toward its destination.

A threat model states what needs protection, who may attack it, what the attacker can observe or change, and which components remain trusted. A passive observer records traffic. An active intermediary can also delay, discard, modify or inject it. An off-path attacker usually has to guess hidden connection values to make an injected message acceptable. A compromised endpoint can access data after the network encryption terminates.

Confidentiality protects message contents from unauthorized readers. Integrity protects against unauthorized changes, and authentication associates a message or peer with a key or identity. Availability concerns whether legitimate users can obtain service. Freshness concerns whether a message belongs to the current exchange. These goals require separate checks: an authentic old request can still repeat an unwanted transaction.

The cryptographic algorithm can be public; the secret key supplies the protected knowledge. For a uniformly random k-bit key, exhaustive search has 2^k candidates and takes about 2^(k−1) trials on average. This average assumes an arbitrary order of distinct guesses and a way to recognize the right key. Password-derived keys inherit the password search space as well as the derivation cost.

Attacker access matters when interpreting a cryptographic claim. In a known-plaintext attack, some plaintext and matching ciphertext are available. Chosen-plaintext access lets an attacker request encryption of selected messages; chosen-ciphertext access lets an attacker submit selected ciphertexts to a decryption interface under the stated restrictions. Secure designs specify the attack model instead of relying on a hidden algorithm.

Layer boundaries identify where protection ends. Wi-Fi encryption protects the radio link to the access point. TLS can protect the application stream from the browser to the website even when intermediaries control routing. The path still reveals traffic timing, packet lengths and destination addressing to relevant observers. A useful analysis names the exact protected span and then follows what each actor receives.
example: A document service sends a file through a café access point. A passive observer can measure when packets arrive. With correctly authenticated TLS and uncompromised endpoints, the file contents remain protected across that access point. If the observer discards every packet, the connection loses availability. These outcomes concern different goals and can occur during the same connection.

questions.prompt: A router on the path can discard packets but cannot obtain the TLS traffic keys. Which security goal can it directly defeat, and which observations can it still make?
questions.hint: Trace both the delivery decision and the headers outside TLS.
questions.answer: It can defeat availability by dropping traffic. It can observe IP addressing, packet sizes and timing at its position. Correct TLS record protection preserves application confidentiality and integrity against that router under the stated key and endpoint assumptions.

questions.prompt: A protocol accepts an old, correctly authenticated transfer request twice. Identify the missing check and describe one concrete state value that supplies it.
questions.hint: The second copy carries the same bytes and tag.
questions.answer: The receiver needs a freshness or replay check. It can authenticate a monotonically increasing transaction number and retain the largest accepted value, rejecting reused or older numbers according to the protocol. Reliable state handling across retries and restarts is part of this design.

title: Symmetric encryption and modes
heading: Track the input to every block operation
problem: three ways a block cipher turns a long plaintext into ciphertext, and where repeated inputs leak information.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='encryption-modes-title' viewBox='0 0 720 360'><title id='encryption-modes-title'>Track the input to every block operation</title><defs><marker id='encryption-modes-arrow' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='7' refY='4' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z' fill='#176a70'/></marker></defs><g font-family='system-ui, sans-serif' font-size='17' fill='#17343d'><text x='25' y='30' font-size='17' text-anchor='start'>A block cipher needs a rule for longer messages</text><rect x='25' y='65' width='200' height='105' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><text x='125.0' y='92' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>ECB</text><text x='125.0' y='117' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Cᵢ = Eₖ(Pᵢ)</text><text x='125.0' y='142' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Equal blocks repeat</text><rect x='260' y='65' width='200' height='105' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><text x='360.0' y='92' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>CBC</text><text x='360.0' y='117' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Cᵢ = Eₖ(Pᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ₋₁)</text><text x='360.0' y='142' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>C₀ = IV</text><rect x='495' y='65' width='200' height='105' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><text x='595.0' y='92' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>CTR</text><text x='595.0' y='117' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Sᵢ = Eₖ(counterᵢ)</text><text x='595.0' y='142' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Cᵢ = Pᵢ ⊕ Sᵢ</text><text x='360' y='215' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'>Repeated CTR keystream cancels under XOR</text><text x='360' y='252' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>C ⊕ C′ = (P ⊕ S) ⊕ (P′ ⊕ S) = P ⊕ P′</text><text x='360' y='305' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'>CBC: unpredictable IV.   CTR / OFB: never repeat a keystream.</text></g></svg>
explanation: Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key, or directly related secret keys, for encryption and decryption. AES is a block cipher: for a fixed key it permutes 128-bit blocks. AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 name the key lengths in bits; all three use the same 128-bit block size. A mode of operation specifies how to process a message spanning several blocks.

In electronic codebook mode, Cᵢ = Eₖ(Pᵢ). Here Pᵢ and Cᵢ are plaintext and ciphertext block i, and Eₖ is block encryption under key K. Equal input blocks produce equal output blocks under that key. A known plaintext block therefore labels every identical ciphertext block, even when the attacker cannot find the key. A repeated block reveals equality rather than every byte of an unfamiliar block.

Cipher block chaining uses C₀ = IV and Cᵢ = Eₖ(Pᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ₋₁); decryption uses Pᵢ = Dₖ(Cᵢ) ⊕ Cᵢ₋₁. The symbol ⊕ means bitwise exclusive OR, and Dₖ reverses Eₖ. CBC encryption needs a fresh unpredictable initialization vector, available to the receiver. With the same key and IV, matching plaintext prefixes give matching ciphertext prefixes. After a different preceding ciphertext block, equal plaintext blocks generally encrypt differently.

CBC also illustrates malleability. Replacing IV with IV ⊕ Δ changes the first decrypted block to P₁ ⊕ Δ. Changing a preceding ciphertext block similarly flips chosen bits in the next plaintext block while disrupting the modified block’s own decryption. An authenticated construction binds the IV and ciphertext so the receiver rejects such edits. A checksum whose value an attacker can recompute supplies no keyed authentication.

Counter mode encrypts a sequence of distinct counter blocks to make keystream blocks Sᵢ, then computes Cᵢ = Pᵢ ⊕ Sᵢ. Counter blocks must be unique across all messages using a key. Output feedback mode instead repeatedly encrypts its internal state to produce a keystream; repeating its key and IV repeats that stream. For either reused stream, C ⊕ C′ = P ⊕ P′. Knowledge of P then reveals the corresponding bytes of P′. Fig. 2 lets you trace this cancellation with adjustable small values.

CBC needs unambiguous padding when a message is not a whole number of blocks. With PKCS#7 padding and a 16-byte block, each added byte equals the number of added bytes. A 20-byte message receives twelve bytes of value 12 and occupies 32 bytes; a 32-byte message receives a full 16-byte padding block. CTR can handle a partial final block without this padding. Encryption modes supply their stated confidentiality properties; message authentication must also be designed into the protocol.
example: For a one-byte illustration, plaintext P = 170 and keystream S = 60 produce ciphertext 150. A second plaintext P′ = 85 using that same stream produces ciphertext 105. XORing 150 and 105 gives 255, equal to 170 ⊕ 85. An observer who knows the first plaintext recovers the second byte as 150 ⊕ 105 ⊕ 170 = 85. These tiny values demonstrate the algebra and provide no cryptographic security.

questions.prompt: Two files use CBC with the same key and IV. Their first two ciphertext blocks match and their third blocks differ. What can you derive about their first three plaintext blocks?
questions.hint: Apply CBC decryption to each block and include its preceding ciphertext input.
questions.answer: The first plaintext blocks match because both C₁ and IV match. The second plaintext blocks match because C₂ and C₁ match. The third plaintext blocks differ: the same preceding C₂ is XORed with decryptions of distinct C₃ blocks, and the block-cipher decryption is a permutation.

questions.prompt: A 16-byte-block CBC format uses PKCS#7 padding. How many ciphertext bytes encode a 31-byte plaintext? What changes for a 32-byte plaintext? Exclude the IV and any authentication tag.
questions.hint: Padding is added even when the message already fills a block.
questions.answer: 31 bytes receive one padding byte, producing 32 ciphertext bytes. 32 bytes receive sixteen padding bytes, producing 48 ciphertext bytes. This count includes only padded ciphertext; a transmitted IV and tag add their own lengths.

Replay handling belongs to the protocol.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A payment message needs both privacy and trustworthy contents. Authenticated encryption with associated data, abbreviated AEAD, takes a secret key K, a nonce N, plaintext P and associated data A. It returns protected ciphertext and an authentication tag. The receiver supplies the corresponding values to authenticated decryption, which returns plaintext or failure.

Associated data remains visible while being covered by authentication. It can hold a record type, routing context or protocol version that the receiver needs before processing the contents. Authentication binds that context to the ciphertext. If an attacker changes an authenticated field, verification fails except with the scheme’s forgery probability under its security assumptions.

For a nonce-based construction such as AES-GCM, each encryption nonce must be unique for its key. A nonce can be a carefully managed record counter; it does not need to be secret. Reusing a nonce can repeat the encryption keystream and damage authentication as well. Separate direction-specific keys or separate nonce spaces keep the two senders from accidentally encrypting different messages with the same key and nonce.

A protocol using separate encryption and a message authentication code must specify the composition and which exact bytes are authenticated. Encrypt-then-MAC authenticates ciphertext and required context before releasing the decrypted data. A standard AEAD construction supplies a reviewed interface for this task. Padding errors and authentication errors also need careful handling so the interface does not become a decryption oracle.

Key possession and identity connect at the handshake. A valid tag establishes that the record is consistent with a holder of the relevant symmetric key; the authenticated key-establishment protocol explains whose key that is. In a shared-key group, every holder may generate valid tags. The application’s authorization rules decide what a successfully authenticated peer may request.

A copied authentic record can pass the same cryptographic check. The receiver therefore checks freshness with authenticated sequence numbers, a replay window, a challenge, or another protocol-specific rule. The rule must account for retransmission and state recovery. Even a correctly authenticated record can contain an invalid application request, so application validation follows successful record verification.
example: A sensor record authenticates a visible device identifier and sequence number while encrypting a temperature. Altering the identifier invalidates the tag. Replaying an unchanged old packet can preserve its valid tag, so the receiver also checks that the authenticated sequence number falls in its permitted fresh range.

questions.prompt: Does a valid authentication tag alone establish that a packet is fresh?
questions.hint: Consider an unchanged copy of a previously valid packet.
questions.answer: The copied packet can still verify. The protocol must separately check freshness, such as whether an authenticated sequence number has already been accepted.

questions.prompt: A sender encrypts a command and sends its destination account as unauthenticated cleartext. How should an AEAD interface bind the destination to this command while keeping the destination readable?
questions.hint: Decide which input provides integrity for visible context.
questions.answer: Place the destination account in associated data A, with an unambiguous encoding and any other required context. The receiver uses that same A during verification. The tag then binds the visible destination to the encrypted command.

title: Hashes, collisions and message authentication
heading: Choose the right hash property and authentication check
problem: a plain digest, a keyed message authentication code and a signature answering different verification questions.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='hashes-macs-title' viewBox='0 0 720 360'><title id='hashes-macs-title'>Choose the right hash property and authentication check</title><defs><marker id='hashes-macs-arrow' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='7' refY='4' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z' fill='#176a70'/></marker></defs><g font-family='system-ui, sans-serif' font-size='17' fill='#17343d'><text x='25' y='30' font-size='17' text-anchor='start'>Which party can produce the value the receiver checks?</text><rect x='25' y='65' width='200' height='125' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><text x='125.0' y='92' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Plain hash</text><text x='125.0' y='117' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>digest = H(message)</text><text x='125.0' y='142' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Anyone can compute it</text><rect x='260' y='65' width='200' height='125' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><text x='360.0' y='92' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Keyed MAC</text><text x='360.0' y='117' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>tag = MACₖ(message)</text><text x='360.0' y='142' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Key holders compute it</text><rect x='495' y='65' width='200' height='125' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2'/><text x='595.0' y='92' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Digital signature</text><text x='595.0' y='117' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Sign with private key</text><text x='595.0' y='142' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Verify with public key</text><text x='360' y='235' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'>b-bit digest: 2ᵇ possible outputs</text><text x='360' y='270' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'>Any-pair collision probability ≈ 1 − exp[−n(n−1) / 2ᵇ⁺¹]</text><text x='360' y='315' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'>n independent uniform digest samples; this is a birthday model.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A cryptographic hash maps a variable-length message to a fixed-length digest. The same message gives the same digest. A digest can identify a file when the expected digest arrived through a trusted channel. If an attacker controls both a message and its advertised digest, the attacker can replace both. The source and protection of the expected value therefore matter.

Preimage resistance asks whether an attacker given a digest h can find a message m with H(m) = h. Second-preimage resistance starts with a particular message m and asks for a different m′ with the same digest. Collision resistance lets the attacker choose both messages and asks for any distinct pair with equal digests. A short predictable input still allows enumeration even when the hash has strong cryptographic properties.

For an ideal b-bit hash, an unrestricted preimage search takes about 2^b trials, while a collision search reaches useful probability near 2^(b/2) samples. After n independent uniformly distributed digest samples, the birthday approximation gives P(collision) ≈ 1 − exp[−n(n−1)/(2 × 2^b)]. The approximation assumes a sufficiently sparse sample relative to the output space. Fig. 2 varies the digest width and sample count to show why the two search tasks have different costs.

A message authentication code, or MAC, uses a shared secret key. A receiver recomputes or verifies the tag for the exact message and context. Only parties holding that key should be able to create valid tags. Because the receiver also knows the key, a shared-key MAC gives no public proof of which key holder authored a message. Digital signatures use a different key arrangement for publicly verifiable authorship claims.

HMAC uses an inner and an outer hash: HMAC(K,m) = H((K₀ ⊕ opad) ∥ H((K₀ ⊕ ipad) ∥ m)). Here ∥ means byte concatenation, K₀ is the key normalized to the hash block length, and ipad and opad are fixed standardized byte strings. The construction separates the inner and outer processing. A raw prefix tag H(K ∥ m) with a Merkle–Damgård hash such as SHA-256 can permit a length-extension forgery when the attacker can infer the key length and the application accepts the extended encoded message.

Hash speed has different consequences in different tasks. Fast secure hashing helps file verification and HMAC. A password verifier needs a salted, deliberately expensive password derivation function because human-chosen passwords occupy a much smaller search space. MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collision weaknesses, so new designs use an appropriate modern hash and a standard keyed construction. A hash’s output length alone does not establish its security.
example: For a toy 16-bit digest and 300 independent random samples, the birthday estimate is 1 − exp[−300 × 299/(2 × 65,536)] ≈ 0.496. This is the chance of some matching pair among those samples. A uniformly random 16-bit target digest has probability 1/65,536 of matching each independent preimage guess.

questions.prompt: An attacker knows that a SHA-256 digest belongs to a uniformly selected five-digit decimal code. Including leading zeros, how many candidates exist, and what is the average exhaustive-search count?
questions.hint: Count the input space instead of the output space.
questions.answer: There are 10⁵ = 100,000 possible codes. Distinct guesses in an arbitrary fixed order find a uniformly chosen code after (100,000 + 1)/2 = 50,000.5 guesses on average. SHA-256’s 256-bit output does not enlarge this five-digit input space.

questions.prompt: A software mirror supplies a download and its SHA-256 digest over the same attacker-controlled channel. What trusted information would let you verify authenticity?
questions.hint: Ask who can replace the digest and what public or shared key is already trusted.
questions.answer: Use an authenticated expected digest, such as a release manifest signed by a publisher whose public key you already trust, or obtain the digest through an independently authenticated channel. Checking that trusted value binds the received bytes to the publisher’s expected release.

explanation: A software publisher wants strangers to verify an update without giving them the power to forge updates. A digital signature scheme supplies a private signing key and a public verification key. The publisher signs the message’s defined representation. A reader verifies the signature using the corresponding public key. Every key holder must also protect the surrounding process that chooses which files are signed.

Public-key encryption uses a different direction of authority: a sender encrypts to the recipient’s public encryption key, and the recipient decrypts with a private key. A signature authenticates signed data while leaving the data readable unless encryption is added. Modern schemes specify hashing, encoding, randomness and validation rules. Describe the full signature scheme rather than treating all signature algorithms as reversible encryption.

RSA arithmetic illustrates a public/private relationship. Choose primes p and q, set n = pq and φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1), choose e relatively prime to φ(n), and choose d with ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n). The public key includes n and e; the private key includes d and usually other values for efficient computation. For a representative integer 0 ≤ m < n, textbook RSA computes c = m^e mod n and recovers m = c^d mod n. Secure encryption and signatures use standardized encodings such as RSA-OAEP and RSA-PSS around that arithmetic. Factoring n reveals the prime factors and allows recovery of the private exponent, so practical RSA relies on suitably large, securely generated primes as well as the complete standardized scheme.

A valid signature answers a key-based question. The reader still needs to know who owns that verification key. A certificate binds a subject identity and public key under a certificate authority’s signature. A validation chain connects that certificate through permitted issuing authorities to a locally trusted root. The locally configured trust anchor starts the chain; merely receiving a root certificate from a stranger does not create that trust.

Certificate validation includes signatures, the intended name or identity, validity dates, permitted key usage and issuer constraints, plus applicable revocation policy. A leaf certificate signed by a trusted hierarchy can still be for a different hostname. A certificate authenticates the claimed identity according to the issuing policy; it supplies no general guarantee that the application is honest or its content is safe.

The exact signed bytes matter. A signature over a file with a final newline covers different bytes from the same visible text without that newline. Encoding, line endings and formatting must follow the signed format’s canonicalization rules. Verification failure can therefore reveal an accidental transformation as well as malicious editing. Applications should verify using a supported cryptographic library and the exact specified format.
example: As an arithmetic-only RSA example, p = 11 and q = 17 give n = 187 and φ(n) = 160. Choose e = 7 and d = 23 because 7 × 23 = 161 ≡ 1 mod 160. Message representative m = 42 gives c = 42⁷ mod 187 = 15, and 15²³ mod 187 = 42. These tiny primes are immediately factorable; the example teaches the calculation rather than a deployable scheme.

questions.prompt: A signature verifies under a public key downloaded beside the message. What evidence connects that public key to the intended publisher?
questions.hint: Follow the trust chain until you reach information you already trust.
questions.answer: The reader needs an authenticated key binding, such as a certificate chain to an accepted trust anchor with the correct identity and usage, an independently verified key fingerprint, or a previously provisioned publisher key. Verification under an arbitrary attacker-supplied key only establishes consistency with that key.

questions.prompt: A signed text file gains a newline during copying. The words displayed on screen stay the same. What must the verifier check?
questions.hint: Identify the exact input to the signature’s hashing and encoding process.
questions.answer: The verifier must check the exact bytes specified by the signing format. A newly added newline changes those bytes and ordinarily invalidates the signature. A format with explicit canonicalization instead applies its defined normalization before verification.

sourceNotes: Course scope: Public Key Cryptography; certificate chain introduction; cryptographic-tool lab concepts.

title: Key establishment and forward secrecy
heading: Establish fresh traffic keys with an authenticated peer
problem: two peers deriving the same Diffie–Hellman secret while exchanging only public group values.

p = Aᵇ mod p :Bob</text><text x='360' y='280' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Authenticate peers and transcript, then derive traffic keys.</text><text x='360' y='320' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'>Erase fresh exponents after use to support forward secrecy.</text></g></svg>
explanation: Two devices need a shared secret before symmetric protection can begin. Diffie–Hellman key agreement lets each device contribute a fresh private value. In the finite-field illustration, p is a prime modulus and g is a selected group generator. Alice keeps exponent a secret and sends A = g^a mod p. Bob keeps b secret and sends B = g^b mod p. The exchanged A and B are public.

Alice computes B^a mod p, and Bob computes A^b mod p. Both equal g^(ab) mod p. Suitable groups and large secret exponents make recovering the shared value from the public transcript computationally hard under the scheme’s assumptions. Real implementations use standardized groups, validate peer public values and derive separate keys with a key derivation function. Fig. 2 uses small numbers to make each arithmetic step visible.

An active intermediary can replace both public values in an unauthenticated exchange, creating one shared secret with Alice and another with Bob. Authentication binds the peer identities, negotiated choices and exchanged values to the handshake. A certificate and a signature over the relevant transcript can supply this binding. The receiver checks the signature and the certificate’s identity and policy before accepting the intended peer.

RSA key transport takes another approach: one side generates a session secret and sends it encrypted to the other side’s long-term public encryption key. An observer who records this encrypted secret can recover it later if the corresponding private decryption key is stolen. Ephemeral authenticated Diffie–Hellman instead uses fresh exponents for the session and a long-term key to authenticate the exchange.

Forward secrecy protects recorded past sessions against later compromise of a long-term authentication key, assuming the ephemeral secrets and traffic keys have been erased and the underlying agreement remains hard. Endpoint compromise during the session can expose its live keys. Forward secrecy also depends on the actual negotiated key exchange; a certificate’s RSA public key can authenticate an ephemeral exchange without being used for RSA key transport.

Quantum algorithms change these hardness assumptions. Shor’s algorithm gives a sufficiently capable quantum computer an efficient route to factoring and discrete logarithms, affecting RSA and conventional finite-field or elliptic-curve key exchange. Grover’s generic search gives an idealized square-root reduction in search steps, with substantial implementation costs. Post-quantum mechanisms use other mathematical problems. Protection against a malicious endpoint still requires the same identity, implementation and trust analysis.
example: For a toy exchange, p = 23, g = 5, a = 6 and b = 15 give A = 8 and B = 19. Alice computes 19⁶ mod 23 = 2; Bob computes 8¹⁵ mod 23 = 2. The secret value 2 is then conceptually an input to a key derivation function. These tiny parameters allow exhaustive recovery and serve only to trace the equation.

questions.prompt: A session uses fresh Diffie–Hellman exponents and authenticates the handshake with a long-term signature key. Years later, the signature key leaks. Under what assumptions do recorded old session contents remain confidential?
questions.hint: Distinguish the key that signed the exchange from the secrets that generated its traffic keys.
questions.answer: Past contents remain confidential if ephemeral exponents and traffic keys were erased, the observer did not compromise the live endpoints or otherwise obtain those secrets, and the key-agreement and record-protection assumptions still hold. The later signature key can enable future impersonation but does not itself reveal the old ephemeral shared secret.

questions.prompt: An intermediary replaces Alice’s public DH value before Bob receives it. What exact information should handshake authentication bind?
questions.hint: Include values whose substitution changes the key or the claimed participants.
questions.answer: Bind the public key-exchange values, identities or role context, and negotiated protocol choices into an authenticated transcript, with freshness as required by the protocol. Bob must verify that authentication using a key bound to Alice or to the intended authenticated peer. This connects the derived key to the intended exchange.

title: Wi-Fi, DHCP and ARP trust
heading: Trace association, configuration and local delivery separately
problem: a device establishing a radio link, obtaining network settings and resolving a local next hop.

ARP resolution</text><text x='595.0' y='117' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>IPv4 address ↔ MAC</text><text x='595.0' y='142' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Reach local next hop</text><text x='595.0' y='167' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>Validated bindings</text><line x1='230' y1='130' x2='255' y2='130' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#link-security-arrow)'/><line x1='465' y1='130' x2='490' y2='130' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#link-security-arrow)'/><text x='360' y='245' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'>Radio encryption ends at the access point.</text><text x='360' y='280' font-size='17' text-anchor='middle'>TLS can continue to the application’s authenticated endpoint.</text><text x='360' y='320' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'>A usable network path and a trusted application identity are separate checks.</text></g></svg>
explanation: A new laptop needs several pieces of information before it can load a page. Wi-Fi association establishes a local radio connection. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, or DHCP, can assign the laptop an IP address, a DNS resolver and a default gateway. Address Resolution Protocol, or ARP, maps an IPv4 next-hop address to a local media access control address, called a MAC address. Each stage has its own trust assumptions.

WPA2-Personal derives a pairwise master key from the shared password and network name. Its four-way handshake uses the client and access-point nonces and MAC addresses to derive pairwise keys and confirm possession. The resulting key material separates handshake confirmation, key protection and traffic protection. An observer with the shared password and the required captured handshake can derive that session’s pairwise keys. A weak password can also be tested against captured handshake evidence offline.

WPA2-Enterprise uses an authentication method through an authentication server rather than giving all users the same password-derived master key. For example, a correctly configured TLS-based EAP method validates the authentication server and establishes key material for the client’s association. Client certificate and server-name validation settings matter: accepting an impostor authentication server can expose credentials or permit an unintended connection, depending on the EAP method.

WPA3-Personal uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, or SAE, a password-authenticated key exchange. Its design resists the simple passive offline password test available from a WPA2-Personal handshake and supports forward secrecy for the established association. Security conclusions depend on the mode actually negotiated, including whether transition settings allow WPA2, and on implementation correctness. Radio encryption protects the client-to-access-point span; application protection continues independently beyond the access point.

DHCP discovery and offers commonly occur before the client has a trusted authenticated server relationship. A rogue local server can race a legitimate offer and supply an attacker-controlled DNS resolver or gateway. DHCP snooping constrains which switch ports may supply server messages. It can also build address bindings used by other controls. These defenses depend on correct switch configuration and trusted uplinks.

ARP announcements and replies similarly need an authenticated basis or enforcement policy. A local attacker can claim that a gateway IP belongs to the attacker’s MAC address, redirecting traffic through that device. Dynamic ARP inspection checks claims against permitted bindings, often learned through DHCP snooping; static mappings are another option in managed settings. End-to-end TLS still checks the intended server identity and protects records even when a local intermediary forwards the connection.
example: A laptop uses gateway 192.0.2.1 in a teaching network. A rogue ARP reply maps that address to another local device’s MAC. Frames for the gateway then reach the rogue device, which may forward or drop them. Correctly authenticated TLS keeps the application’s encrypted contents protected across that forwarding path, while the attacker gains observation of traffic metadata and control over delivery.

questions.prompt: A café gives every visitor the WPA2-Personal password. A visitor records another client’s complete required handshake. What information makes that client’s link keys derivable, and where does TLS protection end?
questions.hint: List the password-derived input and the public handshake inputs, then trace the two encryption spans.
questions.answer: The visitor has the shared password and network name plus captured nonces and client/AP MAC addresses, supplying the inputs for the WPA2-Personal pairwise derivation. This can expose that association’s link traffic under the stated capture and configuration assumptions. TLS continues from its client endpoint to its authenticated server endpoint, so properly protected application contents retain that separate end-to-end protection.

questions.prompt: A new host accepts a rogue DHCP offer advertising an attacker-controlled resolver. The browser then reaches an impostor site address for a legitimate hostname. Which later check can detect that impostor?
questions.hint: Separate selecting an address from authenticating the named service.
questions.answer: TLS server authentication checks a valid certificate chain for the hostname the browser intended, along with handshake authentication. An attacker who only controls DHCP and DNS lacks the legitimate server’s required credentials, so normal validation rejects impersonation. The attacker can still disrupt delivery or observe traffic at its position.

heading: Locate the protection boundary inside the packet path
problem: an IPsec tunnel protecting an inner packet between gateways while an outer IP header routes it across the network.

original outer IP header for routing.</text><text x='360' y='325' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'>IKE authenticates peers and derives the tunnel’s keys.</text></g></svg>
explanation: IP supplies routing addresses and packet delivery without built-in authentication of the sender’s claimed source address. IPv4 has 32-bit addresses; IPv6 has 128-bit addresses. A prefix /r fixes the first r bits, leaving 2^(w−r) addresses in a w-bit address space before any address-use reservations. A source address therefore describes a claimed return location; cryptographic authentication or network enforcement supplies stronger evidence.

IPsec adds security associations containing keys, algorithms, sequence handling and policy for protected traffic. Encapsulating Security Payload, or ESP, can provide confidentiality and integrity according to the chosen suite. Authentication Header, or AH, supplies authentication over specified packet fields without encrypting the data. Internet Key Exchange, or IKE, negotiates authenticated key establishment and association parameters. The configured peer identities and accepted credentials determine who can establish protection. An authenticated ESP sequence number and an anti-replay window can reject duplicates and packets outside the receiver’s accepted range for that association.

In transport mode, ESP protects the transport payload while the original outer IP header remains available for routing. In tunnel mode, ESP protects an entire inner IP packet and a new outer IP header identifies the tunnel endpoints. A site-to-site tunnel therefore protects the gateway-to-gateway span. The original hosts’ paths to their gateways need their own protections if the same confidentiality goal extends there.

A remote-access VPN similarly shifts which intermediary observes traffic. The local network sees the VPN connection and its traffic pattern; the VPN endpoint can see the traffic after its tunnel protection ends, including destination metadata. Application TLS may remain encrypted through that provider. In a chain, provider one terminates its tunnel before forwarding into provider two’s tunnel. With nested tunnels, the client creates an inner tunnel carried inside an outer one. Fig. 2 traces which endpoint removes each layer. Independence, collusion, routing and endpoint configuration determine the resulting visibility.

Source-address validation constrains spoofing at network boundaries. A customer-facing router can admit only source prefixes that customer may legitimately send, and a network’s outbound policy can enforce its permitted source ranges. Filtering depends on topology: asymmetric routing and multihoming require care when choosing reverse-path checks. A NAT mapping or an IPv6 address length supplies no replacement for a deliberate firewall policy; both protocol stacks need appropriate protection. Although a large IPv6 address space makes blind exhaustive scanning costly, DNS names, predictable address patterns and observed traffic can reveal active addresses. Attackers can also stress finite per-address tracking or neighbor-cache entries by triggering work for many addresses.

ICMP supplies diagnostics and errors, including Echo replies, Time Exceeded and Packet Too Big messages. Traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL or hop limit; expiring probes can trigger replies that reveal portions of the path. The timing measures that probe’s round trip, including return routing and device response behavior. A missing reply may reflect filtering or rate limits. Selective ICMP handling preserves useful functions such as path-MTU discovery while controlling unwanted traffic.
example: A gateway tunnel carries a packet from inner source 192.0.2.10 to inner destination 198.51.100.20. An observer between gateways sees the outer gateway addresses and encrypted payload size/timing. After the exit gateway decrypts the inner packet, it can forward using the inner destination. TLS inside that packet keeps its application data protected until the TLS endpoint.

questions.prompt: A company encrypts traffic only between its two office gateways using ESP tunnel mode. Which addresses must remain visible between those gateways, and which span needs an additional protection decision?
questions.hint: Follow the routing header before decryption and then the path inside each office.
questions.answer: The outer source and destination gateway addresses remain visible so routers can deliver the tunnel packet. The inner addresses and payload can be encrypted by ESP. The host-to-gateway paths inside each office fall outside this gateway tunnel’s protection and need their own protection decisions, such as trusted local links or application TLS.

questions.prompt: A traceroute probe expires at hop 4 and receives an ICMP Time Exceeded response after 24 ms. What does that number measure, and what does an absent response from hop 5 establish?
questions.hint: Include the return path and the device’s choice to answer.
questions.answer: 24 ms measures the elapsed round trip from sending that probe to receiving that ICMP response, including forward travel, response processing and return travel. An absent hop-5 response establishes that no response arrived within the observation window. Filtering, rate limiting, loss, return-path behavior or the device’s response policy can all affect the observation.
